First listed 2025-11-03 · episode or wrap

Inside the Cannabis Comeback: How One Company is Beating a Broken Market | The Real Eisman Playbook

Eisman discloses a speculative Glass House holding and explores a low-cost greenhouse producer's profitability, raid recovery and federal-reform upside with management. Production recovery and eventual NYSE listing have evidence, but cash generation remained weak and broad interstate/export upside was conditional. The important legal distinction is that Schedule III alone does not open unrestricted trade; Farrar explicitly qualifies Kazan's earlier overstatement.

The conditional relationship follows from the explicit assumptions; it does not establish that those assumptions hold in observed markets.

Conditional reasoning

Lower competitive prices compress high-cost margins first. Lower costs preserve a wider operating cushion, while fewer fixed debt payments reduce cash breakeven and default exposure.

  • Products are sufficiently substitutable and producers compete on price.
  • Low-cost producers can supply additional volume.
  • Debt creates fixed obligations regardless of sales prices.

How he reasons here

  • Separate a low-cost operating thesis from a policy catalyst.
  • Normalize seasonal costs, nonrecurring profits and disputed taxes before calculating ROE.
  • Model volume, realized price and margin separately; more production need not mean more cash.
  • Distinguish state permission, federal registration, exchange eligibility and export permits.
  • Treat management superlatives and illustrative capacity revenue as assumptions rather than verified forecasts.
  • Check whether commodity competition erodes the price spread underlying expansion plans.

Tools and charts discussed

Mentioned in the transcript; visual charts have not all been inspected.

  • Gross, operating and adjusted EBITDA margins
  • Production recovery versus OCF
